solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: the surface wants a reason or excuse; read literally, what provides grounds is a mill, as a coffee mill turns out grounds
the thing being ground is talk, so the mill is one that processes hearsay

explanation.surface: Someone asks who supplies the excuse for all the tittle-tattle.
explanation.walkthrough: Grounds means reasons in the surface, but coffee grounds come out of a mill; a mill that grinds out gossip is the idiom wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the rumour mill is the informal chatter network that keeps producing fresh gossip.

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so we go by the sound of the word

parts.note: to rouse is to stir up or provoke

explanation.surface: A plain-spoken person stirs up arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: This ROWS is the quarrel word that rhymes with cows, not the one meaning lines, so it sounds exactly like ROUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rows are noisy quarrels, so disputes in the plural.

parts.note: March is one of the months
ago = in the past, gone by

explanation.surface: A note that a military inspection took place a month back.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a date, but 'one month' is just any month that fits, and 'ago' is an adverb standing for the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a march past is a parade of troops past a saluting or reviewing officer.

clue.text: He made them run off and run a lot

definitions.note: The definition is a noun, the answer a phrase describing it: a lot at auction is under the hammer.

indicators.note: off as in gone wrong, out of its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A bully chased people away and then ran a great deal himself.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two runs: the first is part of the letters to shuffle, the second is just R, added to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose, cryptic sense: an auction lot is the thing that goes under the hammer.

indicators.note: one thing straddles another by sitting astride it, so it goes around it

parts.note: mug is slang for face
S is the standard abbreviation for small
tan is a light brown

explanation.surface: A rider's face is seen astride a little brown pony.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse and 'straddling' belong in one riding image, which is why the container indicator hides well; 'small brown horse' also wants to be a single definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a mustang is a wild horse of the American West.

parts.note: the code for Los Angeles International
a ness is a headland, as in Sheerness; the possessive just joins the parts

explanation.surface: Blame for a failure is pinned on the boss of an American airport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a manager but is a geographical head, a promontory, which place names often call a ness.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: laxness is slackness or carelessness about duty.

clue.text: In Greece, walk from Athens to Argos

indicators.note: the answer is taken from the letters of the words that follow

parts.note: the last letter of the first city, all of 'to', and the first letter of the second

explanation.surface: Directions for a hike between two ancient Greek cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The journey between the cities is a red herring; the answer sits across the join of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek-specific term: a stoa was a covered colonnaded walkway in an ancient Greek city.

clue.text: Do not put up with one having cold

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up turns it bottom to top

parts.note: taken as it stands
I is the Roman numeral one
C = cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to tolerate a person with a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do not' reads as an order, but Do is the definition: in tonic sol-fa, doh is the keynote of the scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term: in sol-fa, do (doh) names the first note of the scale, the tonic.

parts.note: the surface wants dizzy, scatterbrained people; the setter means people whose heads of hair are light in colour
Cinders is Cinderella, named for sitting among the ashes of the fire

explanation.surface: A dig at scatterbrained people compared to a pantomime heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light-headed' suggests dizzy, but it means pale-haired; Cinderella's name comes from cinders, so her colour is ash.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: ash blondes have pale greyish-fair hair, light heads the colour of Cinders's ashes.

clue.text: Perhaps careless, spread and breathe fire

indicators.note: letters spread about are scattered into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dragon's instructions: be reckless, fan out and blow flames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that careless is only one shade of the answer; 'and' is part of the letters, not a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a featherbrained person is silly and scatty, which often makes them careless.

indicators.note: heard over the airwaves, so only the sound counts

parts.note: spun round and round

explanation.surface: Every listener switched the radio on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on the radio' reads as switching a set on; instead 'turned' is the word for spun, spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'the whole world knows' means everybody knows.

clue.text: Semiquaver is the next for playing

indicators.note: the letters are there to be played with and rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A music teacher points out which short note comes up next in the score.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-lesson surface keeps 'for playing' looking like performance rather than an instruction to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: Americans call a semiquaver a sixteenth note, being a sixteenth of a whole note.

indicators.note: strange, out of the usual order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd pairing leads to a strange medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'peculiar' is the trick: the first is the instruction, the second is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the answer used as a noun for any manufactured medicine.

parts.note: grave = serious, so the superlative
as in 'have you heard the one about...'

explanation.surface: A solemn joke carved in stone as a tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joke' is the hard part: a comedian's 'good one' is a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a stone marking a grave is a memorial to the person buried there.

parts.note: the surface wants the child caught in the middle of a game; the setter means a greedy hog of a person
in the middle of the road, where a selfish driver sits

explanation.surface: A reference to piggy in the middle, a children's game of keep-away.
explanation.walkthrough: Piggy in the middle is a British playground game where one child tries to catch a ball thrown over their head; here the piggy is a driver hogging the centre of the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: a road hog drives selfishly, taking the middle of the road for themself.

parts.note: the surface wants staying away from home; the setter means staying out cold, asleep
late into the morning, not late at night

explanation.surface: A reveller is told to keep partying till late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay out late' suggests a night on the town; read it as staying unconscious until late in the morning, in bed at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: to sleep in is to stay asleep past the usual time of getting up.

parts.note: for, in favour of
a joining together

explanation.surface: A disturbance breaks out in support of a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riot' looks like a street protest, which fits the union surface, but it is a riot of colour, an abundance.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a riot of flowers is a lavish abundance of them.

indicators.note: the word is left without its end

parts.note: to check over
a bunker is a storage bin, as for coal; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Mountaineers inspect a half-built shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbers' suggests mountaineers, and 'bunker' a shelter or golf hazard, but they are climbing plants and a storage bin.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: vetches are leguminous plants that climb by tendrils.

clue.text: Animal, in some ways American, reared

indicators.note: in a down clue, rearing up turns the whole thing bottom to top

parts.note: lanes are ways, routes
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A creature that in certain respects is American raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal' looks like a noun, a creature, but it is the adjective, as in animal passions; the whole assembly is flipped, not just one part.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in adjective form: animal appetites are bodily, fleshly ones.

clue.text: A doctor stood as a theologian

parts.note: taken as it stands
Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree
stood up

explanation.surface: A physician once stood in for a churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stood' is the past of stand up; St Ambrose was a fourth-century bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church, which neatly echoes 'doctor'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: St Ambrose is one of the great early Christian theologians.

clue.text: He loved Sebastian — a ridiculous notion

parts.note: taken as it stands

indicators.note: absurd, out of sense and order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the idea of a love for Sebastian as absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Twelfth Night the sea captain Antonio is devoted to Sebastian, Viola's twin.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the character in Twelfth Night whose devotion to Sebastian drives his story.

parts.note: the surface wants minor difficulty; the setter means trouble on a tiny scale, a fuss over nothing
the surface wants trouble building up; the setter means tea brewing in a cup

explanation.surface: A warning that minor difficulties are on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brewing' suggests trouble building, but it is tea brewing, and a tempest in the cup is little because the fuss is trivial.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a storm in a teacup is a great fuss over a trivial matter.

parts.note: decimal means based on ten, so read the answer as two words describing it
the straight definition

explanation.surface: A remark that decimals crop up in lots of situations.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as OF TEN, which is what decimal means: counting in tens.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that happens in many cases happens frequently.

definitions.meaning: a trout-like fish of cold lakes
a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day

explanation.surface: A note about eating fish every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb; it is a noun, the British word for a cleaning woman, also called a charwoman.
explanation.definitionFit: A char is a fish related to the trout, and a char (charwoman) is a daily cleaner.

definitions.meaning: starting to go sour, like milk

explanation.surface: A car rounds a bend and leaves the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going off' reads as leaving the road; it is milk going sour.
explanation.definitionFit: A car cornering is literally on the turn; milk on the turn is starting to go off.

indicators.note: reported speech is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: an old word for no

explanation.surface: A question whether a horse can make a sound, given no report of one.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 refers to the answer at 4 Down, MUSTANG, a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by reference: the cry a horse makes, the horse being the answer to 4.

indicators.note: letting go of a letter takes it out of the word

parts.note: Ernie Wise was half of Morecambe and Wise, a much-loved British comedy double act
the Roman numeral, removed

explanation.surface: Advice that the wise course is to set a bird free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wise' looks like an adjective but is a surname, so the capital W is doing honest work.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a crossword favourite among birds.

parts.note: the surface wants the article; the setter means blood group A
someone who supplies it; 'perhaps' because group A is only one possibility

explanation.surface: A tentative description of someone who supplies things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like the indefinite article but is a blood group, so an 'A provider' gives type A blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: someone who gives group A blood is a provider of A, one kind of blood donor.
